intro.html: Odd things come in many kinds, and English has a word for each. Some words describe how strange something is, from mildly peculiar to wildly bizarre and outlandish. Some describe people and methods that break the usual pattern (eccentric, unorthodox, idiosyncrasy). Some describe things that don’t fit or break the rule (incongruous, anomaly, aberration), and one describes the never-before-seen (unprecedented).
Roots help here: ec-centric = out of the center; ab-err-ation = wandering away; an-omaly = not even, not regular; un-pre-cedented = with nothing going before it.

words.def: strange or odd; also, belonging only to one person or place
words.ex: Grandpa has the {peculiar} habit of putting pickles on his ice cream.
words.ctx: The fish is {peculiar} to this one lake; scientists have searched every other river and pond in the region and never found it anywhere else.
words.etym: From Latin peculiaris, “of one’s own property,” from peculium (private property); the sense “strange” came later.
words.note: In “peculiar to,” it means belonging only to: a custom peculiar to the island.

mn.text: Grandpa Gus orders a scoop of vanilla and asks for a pickle on top. Ivy stares. How {peculiar}!

scene.alt: A grandfather happily eats an ice cream cone with a pickle on top while a girl stares.

words.def: odd in behavior in a harmless, quirky way
words.ex: The {eccentric} inventor wore one red sock and one green sock every day.
words.ctx: The neighbors thought old Mr. Pell was {eccentric}, since he walked his pet turtle on a leash, but they also thought he was the kindest man on the street.
words.etym: From Greek ekkentros, “out of the center”: ek (out of) + kentron (center). It first described orbits that were off-center.

mn.text: Professor Edwin wears a wizard hat to the park and walks his turtle on a leash. He is a bit off-center but perfectly harmless: {eccentric}.

scene.alt: An old professor in a wizard hat happily walks a turtle on a leash in the park.

words.ex: Every morning, the cat performs a {bizarre} trick: riding the dog like a horse around the yard.
words.ctx: At first the inventor’s machine looked {bizarre}, a tangle of pipes, bells and bicycle wheels, but it turned out to make perfect pancakes.
words.note: Bizarre (very strange) is not bazaar (a market).

mn.text: At the bazaar, one stall sells socks for snakes. It is the most {bizarre} stall in the whole market.

scene.alt: At a market stall, a seller holds out a sock for a snake while a girl stares in shock.

words.ex: As usual, Rex arrived at the picnic in an {outlandish} outfit: a rainbow cape and swim fins.
words.ctx: The excuse was so {outlandish} that no one believed it: Max claimed a seagull had flown off with his homework and dropped it in the lake.
words.etym: From Old English utlendisc, “foreign”: out + land. It once meant simply “from another country.”

mn.cue: OUT-LANDISH: from OUT of this LAND
mn.text: Rex strolls into the picnic in a rainbow cape, goggles and a big helmet, an outfit from some faraway land. It is {outlandish}.

scene.alt: A man in a pink cape, goggles and a helmet dances into a picnic while a grandmother gapes.

words.def: not following the usual ways of doing things
words.ex: For years the chef has used an {unorthodox} method: flipping pancakes with a tennis racket.
words.ctx: Her teaching was {unorthodox}: instead of lectures and worksheets, the class learned fractions by baking bread and history by acting out old trials.
words.etym: From un- (not) + orthodox, from Greek orthodoxos, “having the right opinion”: orthos (straight, correct) + doxa (opinion).

mn.cue: UN-ORTHO: NOT the usual straight way
mn.text: Chef Jamal flips his pancakes with a tennis racket, and every one lands perfectly in the pan. His method is {unorthodox}.

scene.alt: A chef flips a pancake high in the air with a tennis racket while a teen watches in surprise.

words.def: out of place; not fitting in with its surroundings
words.ex: Grandpa’s heavy wool coat looked {incongruous} on the sunny beach among all the swimsuits.
words.ctx: The shiny glass tower looked {incongruous} beside the row of tiny, hundred-year-old wooden cottages, like a robot at a tea party.
words.etym: From Latin incongruus, “not agreeing”: in- (not) + congruus (fitting, agreeing).

mn.cue: IN-CONGRUOUS: a penguin in the desert
mn.text: A penguin waddles across the hot desert sand past a puzzled camel. It is completely out of place: {incongruous}.

scene.alt: A sweating penguin stands in the hot desert as a camel stares at it.

words.def: something that departs from what is normal or expected
words.ex: A snowy day in Miami would be an {anomaly}.
words.ctx: The scientists at first thought the strange reading was an {anomaly}, a glitch in one machine, but every instrument recorded the same signal again the next night.

mn.text: Sheep are not normally purple, so the one purple sheep in Omar’s flock is an {anomaly}.

scene.alt: A puzzled farmer scratches his head at one purple sheep among white sheep.

words.def: a departure from what is normal or right, often a brief one
words.ex: The team’s one loss was an {aberration} in an otherwise perfect season.
words.ctx: Her grades had been excellent for years, so her teachers saw the failed quiz as an {aberration} rather than a sign that something was wrong.
words.etym: From Latin aberrare, “to wander away”: ab (away) + errare (to wander, stray).

mn.text: The train that has arrived at eight o’clock sharp every day for ten years is two hours late today. That one late day is an {aberration}.

scene.alt: A shocked commuter with a briefcase reads a delayed sign at a train station that is always on time.

words.def: a habit or way of behaving all your own
words.ex: One of Uncle Felix’s {idiosyncrasies} is tapping his spoon three times before every meal.
words.ctx: Each member of the band had an {idiosyncrasy}: the drummer wore two watches, and the singer would drink tea only from a chipped blue cup.
words.etym: From Greek idiosynkrasia, “one’s own temperament”: idios (one’s own) + synkrasis (a mixing together).

mn.cue: IDIO = your OWN: a quirk all your own
mn.text: Uncle Felix taps his spoon on the bowl exactly three times before every meal: tap, tap, tap. It is his own little {idiosyncrasy}.

scene.alt: A man taps his spoon three times on his bowl before eating while a girl giggles.

words.ex: Snow on the beach in July was {unprecedented} in the town’s history.
words.ctx: The young runner’s win was {unprecedented}: in the race’s hundred-year history, no one under fifteen had ever finished in the top ten, let alone first.
words.etym: From un- (not) + precedented, from precedent, “an earlier example,” from Latin praecedere, “to go before.”
words.note: Unprecedented means never happened before, not merely rare.

mn.text: Snow falls on the beach in July, something no one in town has ever seen before. The storm is {unprecedented}.

scene.alt: A boy in sunglasses gasps at a snowman on the beach in July.

head: word
what is odd about it
rows: strange, from a little to wildly
a method that breaks with custom
out of place where it is
a break from the normal pattern

after.html: Bizarre (very strange) and bazaar (a market) sound alike. And unprecedented is stronger than rare: a rare event has happened before, but an unprecedented one never has.

items.q: A town has a flood about once every fifty years. Is this year’s flood unprecedented?
choices: No: floods have happened there before
items.why: Unprecedented means never happened before. A flood that comes every fifty years is rare, but it has a precedent.

choices: The bizarre machine used bells and bicycle wheels to make pancakes.
We bought spices and rugs at the bizarre.
The bizarre opened at nine on Saturday.
Her bizarre was full of shoppers.
items.why: Bizarre means very strange. A market is a bazaar, a different word.

items.q: Eccentric comes from Greek parts meaning…
items.why: Ek (out of) + kentron (center): an eccentric person is a little off-center.

items.q: True or false: a snowman on a sunny beach is an incongruous sight.
items.why: True. Incongruous means out of place, not fitting its surroundings.
